docs.title: The one idea behind the whole course
docs.text: A model produces a score. A clinical decision needs an operating point, calibration, validation on local data, and a named owner for what goes wrong. Most exam questions are asking which of those is missing.

docs.title: 6 · Agentic AI
docs.text:
Lecture 6~20 minTools and loops

A plain language model only writes text. An agent is a language model inside a loop: it asks to use a tool, a program runs the tool, and the result comes back as text the model can reason about.

docs.title: In plain words
docs.text:
• Tool use. The model writes a structured request; the surrounding program executes it; the result is returned to the model.
  • ReAct. Reason → act → observe → repeat, until a stopping condition.
  • Workflow versus agent. The difference is who decides the next step. A workflow has paths coded in advance; an agent lets the model choose based on what it observed.
  • Five workflow patterns. Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimizer.
  • Evaluation. You judge the trajectory (which tools, which steps, was evidence cited) as well as the final answer, and you count cost.

docs.title: Core ideas in one table
docs.text: Term Plain meaning Tool request Model output naming a tool and arguments. Harness / environment The program that executes the tool and returns the observation. Observation The tool's returned result, not something the model imagined. ReAct Interleave reasoning and actions, using observations for the next step. Few-shot ReAct Example trajectories in the prompt; weights stay fixed. Prompt chaining Fixed sequence of LLM calls, each using the previous output. Routing Classify the request and send it to one specialist handler. Parallelization Independent subtasks run at once, then aggregate. Orchestrator–workers The orchestrator decides at runtime which subtasks are needed. Evaluator–optimizer A generator drafts; an evaluator accepts or returns feedback. Trajectory The full sequence of steps, tool calls and observations.

docs.title: Exam questions
Q1 — Correctly formatted tool requests: is integration complete?
docs.text: Answer. No. A description in the prompt only shows the model how to write a request; it does not prove the request is executed, that arguments are valid, that results are parsed and fed back, or that the tool works on real inputs. You need an end-to-end test: real invocation, schema validation, error handling, and final outputs checked against ground truth on representative cases.

docs.title: Q2 — All paths and exceptions known: workflow or agent?
docs.text: Answer. A predefined workflow. The deciding question is whether the possible paths can be enumerated in advance, not whether the system branches or uses an LLM. An agent adds non-determinism, cost, latency and validation burden with no benefit when the logic is fixed; explicit branches and human-review steps are easier to validate, monitor and audit.

docs.title: Q3 — Parallelization or orchestrator–workers?
docs.text: Answer. Independent, pre-defined summaries → parallelization (all subtasks run, results aggregated). When which reviews are relevant depends on the case → orchestrator–workers (decomposition at runtime). The difference that matters is whether subtasks are fixed in advance or chosen during execution. Orchestration adds coordination cost: more calls and latency, error propagation, non-determinism, harder evaluation, and a synthesizer that must reconcile outputs.

docs.title: Q4 — Evaluator–optimizer acceptance and stopping criteria
docs.text: Answer. Use deterministic checks for facts: every requested finding present, values and units exact, chronology correct, no fabricated values. Use a judge for wording: clarity, coherence, no unsupported claims. Accept only when all deterministic checks pass and the judge is above threshold with no new unsupported claims. Use a revision limit as a fallback, but record "revision limit reached" as a failure, distinct from acceptance; log the reason and validate the evaluator itself against held-out human ratings.

docs.title: Q5 — Design an AI-SCE evaluation of workflow versus agent
docs.text: Answer. Include missing information, inconsistent records, ambiguous findings and routine controls. Record every tool call, step, token and second, and whether missing information was identified and inconsistencies resolved. Compare outcomes (correctness/completeness against ground truth), process (evidence attribution, unnecessary queries, appropriate escalation) and cost. To separate supported from accidentally correct answers, require each statement to cite its source record and inject known inconsistencies.

docs.title: Q6 — Where does the observation come from?
docs.text: Answer. The tool executed by the surrounding program — the model only requests it. The tool description in the prompt is instructions, not an observation.

docs.title: Q7 — What defines ReAct?
docs.text: Answer. Interleaving reasoning and actions, using observations to inform the next step. Not a fixed plan, not a post-hoc explanation, not two separately trained models.

docs.title: Q8 — How do few-shot demonstrations affect ReAct?
docs.text: Answer. They put example trajectories in the context (in-context learning); the weights stay fixed. They do not update parameters or train a controller.

docs.title: Q9 — Why can search reduce hallucinations?
docs.text: Answer. It supplies evidence the model can use in later reasoning, instead of relying on memorised or invented facts. It does not update the weights during the session.

docs.title: Q10 — Workflows versus agents?
docs.text: Answer. Workflows use predefined code paths; agents let the LLM direct the process and tool use. Neither changes the weights.

docs.title: Q11 — Extract → draft → translate: which pattern?
docs.text: Answer. Prompt chaining: sequential LLM calls, each consuming the previous output.

docs.title: Q12 — Classify then send to a specialist handler?
docs.text: Answer. Routing — one path is selected. Parallelization would run several paths and aggregate; that is the classic trap.

docs.title: Q13 — What does a static MCQ benchmark miss?
docs.text: Answer. Deciding what information to request as a consultation develops. Static questions test recall and single-step association, not interactive information gathering.

docs.title: Q14 — Role of agent-based modelling?
docs.text: Answer. To simulate the actions and interactions of participants in a clinical environment, so a system can be tested against realistic behaviour before real deployment.

docs.title: Q15 — After good simulated performance?
docs.text:
Answer. Test real-world impact in clinical studies and monitor after deployment. More simulation or more static questions do not address transfer.

If you remember one thing

Workflow or agent? Ask: can I list the paths in advance? Yes → workflow. No, the next step depends on what the tool returns → agent. Never answer "because it uses an LLM".

docs.title: 6 formulas
docs.text:
\[\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{sens}\cdot p}{\text{sens}\cdot p + (1-\text{spec})(1-p)} \qquad \text{NPV} = \frac{\text{spec}(1-p)}{\text{spec}(1-p)+(1-\text{sens})p}\] \[O/E = \frac{\text{observed deaths}}{\text{mean predicted risk}\times n}\]
  • \(TP=\text{sens}\times P\), \(FN=(1-\text{sens})P\), \(FP=(1-\text{spec})N\), \(TN=\text{spec}\cdot N\).
  • Calibration = predicted vs observed; discrimination = AUROC. O/E needs calibration.
  • Softmax over \(k\) candidates: a score is relative, not a calibrated probability.
  • Mean of readings loses trend: keep slope, min, max, last value.

docs.title: 6 open-question templates
docs.text:
1. "Lower loss but worse facts" → loss averages over common tokens; teacher forcing vs own output; evaluate rare critical facts with blinded clinicians.
  2. "Novel perturbation/drug" → categorical embedding cannot extrapolate; need structure/feature encoder or graph prior.
  3. "Biased/leaky evaluation" → say the specific leakage (future data, patient overlap, balancing, treatment paradox), then the fix (causal inputs, patient-level temporal split, real prevalence, exclude treated negatives).
  4. "Deployment decision" → intended use → unit of output → local validation → operating point (who bears FP vs FN) → monitoring + exit plan → economics.
  5. "Workflow or agent?" → can the paths be enumerated in advance? Yes → workflow; no → agent/orchestrator. Not "does it use an LLM".
  6. "Evaluate an LLM system" → build a test set with injected errors/missing data; measure outcome, process (evidence attribution, unnecessary steps) and cost; distinguish supported from accidentally correct.

docs.title: 5 rules that earn points
docs.text:
1. Name the mechanism, then the consequence. "Attention is permutation-equivariant, therefore both reports give the same averaged vector."
  2. Always separate discrimination from calibration. AUROC is threshold-free; decisions need a threshold and calibration.
  3. Say whose error it is. False positive vs false negative, and who signs off.
  4. State what a result cannot establish. One split, one site, no CIs → no significance, no transportability.
  5. For any model claim, ask: was the reference standard independent of the model? Anchoring and "zero discrepancies" are not validation.

docs.title: The one-line answer to most essay questions
docs.text: The model's score is only a ranking; the clinical decision needs an operating point, calibration, validation on the local case mix, and a named owner for the residual risk.

docs.title: 4 · Models for hospital data
docs.text:
Lecture 4~15 minEHR and metrics

Hospital data are messy records over time: vitals, labs, notes, images. Turning them into one vector per patient is convenient and lossy, and the metrics that look good on a balanced test set can be misleading in a real ward.

docs.title: In plain words
docs.text:
• Patient representation. Static (one row per patient), longitudinal (a sequence over time), or multimodal (text + numbers + images combined).
  • Aggregation loses time. The mean of a vital sign cannot tell a patient who is recovering from one who is deteriorating.
  • Prevalence matters. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test; precision (PPV) also depends on how common the disease is.
  • Labels are treatments. If a patient got a drug because they looked sick, "no shock later" partly reflects the drug, not the patient's baseline risk.
  • Leakage. Using data from after the prediction moment (future lab values, the whole stay) inflates performance.
  • Calibration. AUROC says who is ranked higher; calibration says whether "20% risk" really means 20 out of 100.

docs.title: Core ideas in one table
docs.text:
Term Plain meaning AUROC / discrimination Chance a random positive scores above a random negative. Threshold-free. Calibration Predicted risk versus observed risk; a calibration curve or O/E ratio. PPV / precision Of the flagged patients, how many truly have the disease. Depends on prevalence. NPV Of the unflagged patients, how many are truly negative. O/E ratio Observed deaths ÷ expected deaths (mean predicted risk × n). Treatment paradox Treatment lowers risk, so treated patients look "negative" and the model learns the wrong association. Temporal leakage Using information from the future relative to the prediction time. Dataset shift The deployed population or data pipeline differs from training. Missingness as signal "Was the lab measured?" often encodes clinician concern, not physiology.

Key formulas:

\[\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{sens}\cdot p}{\text{sens}\cdot p + (1-\text{spec})(1-p)} \qquad \text{NPV} = \frac{\text{spec}(1-p)}{\text{spec}(1-p)+(1-\text{sens})p}\] \[O/E = \frac{\text{observed deaths}}{\text{mean predicted risk} \times n}\]

docs.title: Exam questions
Q1 — What is lost by averaging vitals and note embeddings?
docs.text: Answer. Averaging a vital-sign sequence makes a recovering patient and a deteriorating one identical if they share the same mean — the trend disappears. Averaging ten note-chunk embeddings dilutes a single critical finding ("new pleural effusion") to one tenth of the vector. Fixes: keep trend features (slope, min, max, last value, time since abnormal) and per-chunk or attention/max pooling for text. Costs: more features and collinearity, higher overfitting risk, higher dimensionality, more data needed, and attention weights that are harder to interpret.

docs.title: Q2 — Balanced test set, sensitivity = specificity = precision = 0.70, real prevalence 10%?
docs.text: Answer. Sensitivity, specificity and AUROC transfer, because they are conditional on the true class or threshold-free. Precision and accuracy do not: they depend on prevalence. At 10% prevalence, \(\text{PPV} = \frac{0.7 \times 0.1}{0.7 \times 0.1 + 0.3 \times 0.9} = \frac{0.07}{0.34} \approx 0.21\) — about 2 in 10 alarms, not 7. Evaluate on a test set with the real prevalence and ask for calibration and net benefit.

docs.title: Q3 — Treated septic-shock patients labelled negative?
docs.text: Answer. Treatment was given because of early signs, and treated patients who never develop shock are recorded negative, so the model learns "bolus → low risk" (confounding by indication / treatment paradox) and underestimates risk in similar patients. Removing treated patients fixes that bias but creates selection bias: you drop a clinically important subgroup, change the case mix, and the model no longer applies to the patients most likely to be treated.

docs.title: Q4 — Bidirectional LSTM at hour 24 but not for hourly alerts?
docs.text: Answer. At hour 24 the prediction uses the completed 24-hour window, so reading backwards uses no future information — acceptable. For an alert at hour \(t\), a bidirectional model reads the whole stay, including hours after \(t\): retrospective performance is inflated by future leakage, not merely dataset shift. Train and evaluate on causal snapshots truncated at each hour (or unidirectional models), excluding post-event data, then run a prospective silent trial.

docs.title: Q5 — Model A AUROC 0.91 / mean risk 19%; B 0.88 / 8.5%; true mortality 8%?
docs.text: Answer. A discriminates better (0.91 vs 0.88), but B is calibrated (8.5% predicted vs 8% observed). For 200 patients: 16 deaths observed; A predicts \(0.19 \times 200 = 38\), so \(O/E = 16/38 \approx 0.42\) — A massively overestimates risk. Use B (or recalibrate A) for O/E comparison, since O/E requires calibration. The table alone cannot separate quality of care from case-mix differences or statistical uncertainty.

docs.title: Q6 — X-ray subgroup AUROC 0.90 on 1,500 selected patients?
docs.text: Answer. Not justified for everyone. The 0.90 comes from patients who had a chest X-ray in the first 24 hours, and they have 14% mortality versus 7% overall — a sicker, selected group, so the gain is confounded by indication. At a hospital without free-text notes the notes path is unavailable, and applying the X-ray path to all patients is a different distribution: expect a performance and calibration drop. Before use: external validation stratified by available modality, calibration, and a silent trial.

docs.title: Q7 — False-positive rates rise with age: remove age?
docs.text:
Answer. Removing age is unlikely to fix it, because the model reconstructs age from proxies (diagnoses, labs, procedures, notes), so the disparity persists while performance drops. Use subgroup-aware calibration or equalised-odds post-processing, reweighting or more training data for older patients, and audit FPR/TPR by group, calibration curves and net benefit, with clinicians deciding the acceptable trade-off.

If you remember one thing

AUROC tells you who ranks higher. It does not tell you the threshold, the false-positive count, or whether "20%" means 20%. Those are three separate questions.

docs.title: Key figures · one line each
docs.text:
Visual recall10 figuresSay the mechanism

The diagrams that carry most of the exam vocabulary. For each one, the caption is what you should be able to say out loud in the exam — the picture is just the anchor.

docs.title: Attention: queries, keys, values
docs.text: Self-attention: \(q\) from one position is compared with all keys; the softmax weights mix the corresponding values. Self = Q, K, V from the same sequence; cross = Q from one sequence, K/V from another. Trainable projections, unlike the picture's fixed \(v_i\).

docs.title: DINO: two views, one teacher
docs.text: Two augmented views of the same image; the teacher (EMA of the student) produces targets, the student predicts them. The mismatch shown across positions is the cross-view / patch-level matching problem. Slow EMA teacher → stable targets, no collapse.

docs.title: CLIP: contrastive image–text
docs.text: Maximise similarity of the \(N\) matching pairs, minimise the \(N^2-N\) mismatched pairs. Zero-shot classification = compare the image with text prompts; the softmax is over the candidate set, not a calibrated disease probability.

docs.title: How an image enters a language model
docs.text: Matching the length of the vector is not enough: the projection \(W\) and alignment/instruction tuning are what make the LM able to read the visual tokens. Without training, the CLIP vector is out of distribution.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: routing
docs.text: One path is selected. Contrast with parallelization, where all paths run and an aggregator combines them. This is the most common MCQ trap.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: prompt chaining
docs.text: Fixed stages, each consuming the previous output; a gate decides whether to continue. Extract → draft → translate is chaining, not routing.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: parallelization
docs.text: Subtasks are defined in advance and independent; results are aggregated. Use when the decomposition is known before execution.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: orchestrator–workers
docs.text: The orchestrator decides at runtime which subtasks are needed. Extra coordination cost: more calls/latency, error propagation, non-determinism, harder evaluation — justify it only when the paths depend on the case.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: evaluator–optimizer
docs.text: Generator drafts, evaluator checks against criteria and either accepts or returns feedback. Acceptance must be distinguishable from "revision limit reached"; validate the evaluator itself against human ratings.

docs.title: The agent loop
docs.text: Reason → act → observe → repeat until a stop condition. The environment executes tools; observations come from the tool, not from the model's prediction. Use an agent only when the next step depends on observations.

docs.title: 1 · Language models
docs.text:
Lecture 1~15 minFoundations

A language model is a next-word predictor trained on huge amounts of text. Everything else — chatting, summarising, answering — is that one trick repeated.

docs.title: In plain words
docs.text:
• Tokens. Text is cut into pieces (words or word parts). Each piece gets an ID, and each ID becomes a vector (an embedding).
  • Position. The same word means something different at the start or end of a sentence, so a position vector is added to each token embedding.
  • Attention. Each token looks at the other tokens and decides which ones matter. Self-attention means queries, keys and values all come from the same sentence.
  • Causal mask. When generating, a token may only look backwards. Without the mask it would see the answer it is supposed to predict.
  • Training. Predict the next token, compare with the real next token, adjust the weights. The text is its own label, so no human annotation is needed.
  • Adaptation. Prompting (no weight change), RAG (give it documents), fine-tuning or LoRA (change small parts of the weights).

docs.title: Core ideas in one table
docs.text: Term Plain meaning Token A word piece; the unit the model reads and writes. Embedding \(e(x_i)\) The learned vector for a token. Position \(p_i\) A vector saying where in the sequence the token sits. Self-attention Q, K, V from the same sequence. Cross-attention Q from one sequence (e.g. decoder), K/V from another (e.g. encoder). Causal mask Blocks attention to future positions. Teacher forcing Training with the real previous tokens as input. Exposure bias At generation time the model sees its own (possibly wrong) outputs instead. Zero-shot No examples in the prompt. Few-shot A few examples in the prompt; weights stay frozen. LoRA Freeze \(W\) and learn a small update \(\Delta W = BA\) of rank \(r\). RAG Retrieve documents at query time and put them in the prompt.

docs.title: Exam questions
Q1 — Lower average loss but more factual errors?
docs.text: Answer. Loss is an average over all tokens, and most tokens are common boilerplate; rare, critical words (like "pending" versus "normal") barely move the average. Loss is also measured with teacher forcing while generation feeds the model its own output, so errors compound. Lower loss only means the model assigns slightly higher likelihood to observed text on average — it says nothing about rare facts. Greedy decoding does not fix it (it can even pick the more common but wrong phrase); you need a blinded clinician evaluation on a sample stratified to include abnormal and pending results, scoring clinically significant errors.

docs.title: Q2 — Position vectors before or after the Transformer?
docs.text: Answer. Before works. Positions enter with the tokens, so attention can compare "opacity" together with "left" or "right", and the two reports produce different representations. After fails, because self-attention without positions is permutation-invariant: it sees the same set of tokens in both reports, and adding the same position pattern afterwards gives the same averaged vector. Order must be encoded before any operation that mixes tokens.

docs.title: Q3 — Causal mask only in the second layer?
docs.text: Answer. No — the claim is wrong. Layer 1 has full attention, so the representation of "is" already contains information from "absent" before layer 2 applies its mask. The model can then predict "absent" from a representation that has seen it: target leakage. The mask must be causal at every layer.

docs.title: Q4 — Guidelines that change several times a year?
docs.text: Answer. Use RAG: index the current guidelines with document ID, section and version; retrieve the relevant sections per patient; require the answer to cite the document and version, or abstain. Fine-tuning alone fails because the weights freeze a snapshot, cannot cite a version, and underrepresent rare patient groups. It can still fail if retrieval returns an outdated or wrong section, if sections conflict, or if the patient data used for retrieval is incomplete.

docs.title: Q5 — Pooled LoRA adapters or one per department?
docs.text: Answer. Do not adopt the pooled adapter on the aggregate number: department A has 800 of the 1000 letters, so the average is dominated by A and hides an 8–10 point regression in B and C. Report results stratified by department with confidence intervals and require no subgroup degradation. Technically one frozen base model can serve all departments: store one copy of the base weights plus three small adapters (\(\Delta W = BA\), rank \(r\)) and route each request to its department's adapter.

docs.title: Q6 — Where do autoregressive training targets come from?
docs.text: Answer. Each observed token is the target for the position before it: the model predicts token \(i\) from tokens \(1 \ldots i-1\). The text labels itself, so no annotator is needed.

docs.title: Q7 — What does \(p_i\) in \(h_i^{(0)} = e(x_i) + p_i\) supply?
docs.text: Answer. The position of the token in the sequence, so the model can tell the same word at different places apart.

docs.title: Q8 — Self-attention versus cross-attention?
docs.text: Answer. In self-attention, queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, queries come from one sequence and keys/values from another.

docs.title: Q9 — Zero-shot versus few-shot?
docs.text: Answer. Zero-shot gives no task demonstrations; few-shot gives a few examples in the prompt. In both, the weights stay frozen — zero-shot still uses everything learned in pretraining.

docs.title: Q10 — LoRA matrix shapes?
docs.text:
Answer. For \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\) and \(\Delta W = BA\) of rank at most \(r\): \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}\) and \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}\), so the inner dimension \(r\) matches and \(BA\) is \(d \times k\).

If you remember one thing

Loss measures how well the model predicts average text, not whether it gets rare facts right. Say that sentence and you have half of Q1.

docs.title: Multiple choice · answer key
docs.text:
20% of the grade15 minLearn the traps

All Mentimeter questions from lectures 1–2 and 6, with the correct option and the one-line reason. The percentages are what the class voted — where the majority was wrong, that is the trap.

docs.title: Lectures 1–2
1. In autoregressive pretraining, where do the targets come from?
docs.text:
✅ Each observed token serves as the target following its preceding context. (83%)

The text supplies its own labels; no annotator. The "own generated continuation" option is wrong — that would be self-training, not pretraining. Masked-token prediction is BERT-style, not autoregressive.

docs.title: 2. In \(h_i^{(0)} = e(x_i) + p_i\), what is \(p_i\)?
docs.text:
✅ The position of the token in the sequence. (87%)

An embedding of the index, added so the model can distinguish the same token at different locations.

docs.title: 3. What defines self-attention vs cross-attention?
docs.text:
✅ Queries, keys and values come from the same input sequence. (59%)

Cross-attention takes queries from one sequence (e.g. decoder) and keys/values from another (e.g. encoder). Same projection matrix is not required.

docs.title: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting?
docs.text:
✅ Zero-shot supplies no task demonstrations; few-shot supplies examples. (45%)

Both keep the weights frozen. "Uses no pretrained knowledge" is the trap: zero-shot still relies on pretraining.

docs.title: 5. LoRA shapes for \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\), \(\Delta W = BA\) of rank \(r\)?
docs.text:
✅ \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) and \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times k}\). (90%)

Inner dimensions \(r\) must match; the product gives \(d\times k\).

docs.title: 6. Why use different augmented views in visual self-supervision?
docs.text:
✅ They provide related observations from which to learn consistent representations. (83%)

Invariance learning. They do not preserve every clinical detail (augmentation can destroy some) and do not replace an objective.

docs.title: 7. Purpose of a contrastive image–text objective?
docs.text:
✅ Matching pairs get higher similarity than mismatched pairs. (72%)

It is not caption generation, pixel reconstruction, nor independent classification.

docs.title: 8. Image-to-report retrieval vs report generation?
docs.text: ✅ Retrieval selects an existing report; generation predicts a sequence of tokens. (93%)

docs.title: 9. Linear probe \(p = \text{softmax}(Wz + b)\) with fixed \(z = f_\theta(x)\): what is fitted?
docs.text:
✅ \(W\) and \(b\); \(\theta\) is fixed. (58%)

That is the definition of a linear probe.

docs.title: 10. External validation?
docs.text:
✅ Evaluation on independently collected data from outside the development source. (93%)

A random held-out subset of the same dataset is internal validation.

docs.title: Lecture 6
11. In ReAct, where does the observation after a search come from?
docs.text:
✅ The search tool executed by the surrounding program. (36%)

The model requests; the environment executes and returns text. The tool description in the prompt is the trap (41% voted for it).

docs.title: 12. Which description captures ReAct?
docs.text:
✅ Interleave reasoning and actions, using observations to inform subsequent steps. (83%)

Not a plan fixed in advance, not a post-hoc explanation, not two separate trained models.

docs.title: 13. How do few-shot demonstrations influence a ReAct model?
docs.text:
✅ They provide example trajectories in the context while weights stay fixed. (73%)

In-context learning. They do not update parameters or train a controller.

docs.title: 14. Why can external search reduce factual hallucinations?
docs.text:
✅ It supplies evidence the model can use in subsequent reasoning. (100%)

It does not update weights after each search.

docs.title: 15. Main distinction between workflows and agents?
docs.text:
✅ Workflows use predefined code paths; agents let the LLM direct the process and tool use. (74%)

22% picked "workflows keep weights fixed, agents update them" — wrong: neither updates weights.

docs.title: 16. Extract findings → draft summary → translate. Which pattern?
docs.text:
✅ Prompt chaining. (100%)

Sequential LLM calls, each consuming the previous output.

docs.title: 17. Classify a request and send it to one of several specialist handlers?
docs.text:
✅ Routing.

The class voted 100% for parallelization, which is the trap. Parallelization runs independent subtasks and aggregates; routing selects one path. This is the single most likely MCQ trap to reappear.

docs.title: 18. Which capability is least tested by a static medical MCQ benchmark?
docs.text:
✅ Deciding what information to request as a consultation develops. (84%)

Static questions test recall and single-step association; they cannot test interactive information gathering.

docs.title: 19. Role of agent-based modelling in the proposed clinical evaluations?
docs.text:
✅ To simulate the actions and interactions of participants in a clinical environment.

Not to replace the encounter with one fixed Q&A, not to train the next-token predictor, not to rank models by size/speed.

docs.title: 20. An agent performs well in a clinical simulation. What next?
docs.text:
✅ Test real-world impact in clinical studies and monitor after deployment. (90%)

More simulation runs or more static questions do not address transfer.

docs.title: Traps to remember
docs.text: Tempting option Why it is wrong Workflows train/update weights Both workflows and agents keep weights fixed Parallelization for a router Routing selects one path; parallelization runs all Tool description = observation The program executes the tool; the description is only instructions Few-shot = fine-tuning Demonstrations are in context; weights unchanged Zero-shot = no pretrained knowledge It uses pretraining, just no demonstrations Retrieval generates reports Retrieval selects an existing report Balanced test set gives real precision Precision depends on prevalence 0.90 softmax = 90% disease probability Softmax is relative to the candidate set AUROC 0.97 settles the threshold AUROC is threshold-free; the operating point is a clinical decision

docs.title: 3 · Omics models
docs.text:
Lecture 3~20 minSingle cells

Single-cell RNA sequencing counts, for each cell, how many mRNA molecules of each gene it contains. The table is huge, sparse and noisy, so the job is to turn it into a useful vector and to predict what a drug or a gene knockout will do.

docs.title: In plain words
docs.text:
• The data. Rows are cells, columns are ~20,000 genes, values are counts. Most values are zero.
  • Why it is noisy. Some zeros are real (the gene is off), some are technical (the molecule was missed). Cells are also sequenced to different depths, and batches differ by machine, day or lab.
  • scVI. A probabilistic model (VAE) that compresses a cell into a low-dimensional vector while explicitly modelling zeros, library size and batch.
  • scGPT. A Transformer over genes, learning from millions of cells. It gives general-purpose cell embeddings, but does not necessarily beat a model fitted to your dataset.
  • Perturbations (CPA, GEARS). Predict how gene expression changes after a drug or a knockout, including combinations never observed.

docs.title: Core ideas in one table
docs.text: Term Plain meaning scRNA-seq Counts of mRNA per gene per cell. Sparsity / excess zeros Most counts are zero, partly technical. Library size Total counts per cell; varies with sequencing depth. Batch effect Technical differences between experimental batches. ZINB Zero-inflated negative binomial: a gate for extra zeros plus a count distribution. VAE / latent \(z\) Compress each cell to a few numbers, then reconstruct its counts. Zero-shot Use a pretrained model on new data without fitting it. Perturbation A drug, a knockout, or a combination applied to cells. No-Change baseline Predict that expression stays the same; a suspiciously strong baseline. Masked gene prediction Hide a gene's value and predict it from the others — scGPT's training task.

docs.title: Exam questions
Q1 — How does scVI handle the five challenges?
docs.text: Answer. (1) Sparsity/excess zeros: a zero-inflated negative binomial likelihood — a dropout gate for extra zeros plus a negative binomial for counts. (2) Varying library size: the observed total count enters the mean as an explicit scaling factor. (3) Batch effects: batch is a covariate fed to the encoder and decoder, so the latent \(z\) is pushed to capture biology. (4) Biological noise: a probabilistic latent variable sampled from a prior, with dispersion, instead of a single point estimate. (5) Scalability: amortised inference with an encoder network and mini-batch gradient descent, rather than optimising parameters per cell.

docs.title: Q2 — Why is a cell not a sentence of genes?
docs.text: Answer. Gene order is arbitrary and the number of expressed genes varies per cell, so positional information is meaningless and the "sentence" length is not fixed. A cell is a set of genes with expression values, and using gene identity alone throws away the magnitudes and the zeros. Two fixes: embed gene identity plus expression value (normalised), and make the architecture order-invariant (no positional embeddings, attention over a set).

docs.title: Q3 — TP53 with the same expression in two cells?
docs.text: Answer. The initial embeddings are identical: same gene identity and same expression value. The post-Transformer embeddings differ, because self-attention mixes TP53 with the other genes expressed in that cell. That is the point: a gene's representation becomes context-dependent, capturing gene–gene interactions and cell state.

docs.title: Q4 — Frozen scGPT versus dataset-fitted scVI?
docs.text: Answer. Expect the dataset-fitted scVI to integrate batches better and often preserve biology better; a zero-shot foundation model was not trained on this dataset and tends to carry its batch structure. The exception is batch–biology confounding (e.g. cancer and normal in different batches): aggressive batch removal can delete the signal you want, so a model that removes less may preserve more biology — at the cost of leaving batch in. Decide by measuring biological conservation (cell-type separation, marker recovery), not by assuming integration always helps.

docs.title: Q5 — Can CPA predict a completely unseen drug?
docs.text: Answer. Not with standard CPA: each perturbation is a learned embedding, so a drug absent from training has no embedding. Generalisation needs a perturbation representation that transfers — chemical structure/fingerprint features, or training on mechanism classes. If the adversarial weight is zero, the basal state is no longer forced to be perturbation-invariant, so it can absorb drug information; the clean split between "cell state" and "drug effect" breaks and counterfactual predictions for unseen combinations become unreliable.

docs.title: Q6 — Why does GEARS need the perturbation graph \(G_\text{pert}\)?
docs.text: Answer. \(G_\text{gene}\) encodes which genes are co-expressed; \(G_\text{pert}\) encodes which perturbations have similar downstream effects. GEARS propagates information over \(G_\text{pert}\) so the effect of an unobserved knockout can be borrowed from perturbations with similar effects. Using only \(G_\text{gene}\) relates perturbations through co-expression, which is a different relationship, so a never-perturbed gene cannot borrow strength and its predicted knockout collapses to something arbitrary or average.

docs.title: Q7 — MSE 0.05 vs No-Change 0.06 with 50/10,000 genes changing?
docs.text:
Answer. Predicting "no change" is already correct for ~99.5% of entries, so global MSE is dominated by unchanged genes and hides whether the model learned the treatment effect. Evaluate on differentially expressed genes (top-k by effect size), use per-gene standardised errors or delta/correlation between predicted and observed effects, and report MSE on changed genes separately. The 0.05 versus 0.06 gap may be clinically meaningless.

If you remember one thing

In omics, always ask what is held out: a cell, a batch, a perturbation, or a drug never seen. That word decides whether the claim is generalisation or memorisation.

docs.text:
